transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Alex (Redwood SRE), Marta (NovaDocs ML), Samir (NovaDocs Platform), Jordan (CTO)
Shared: https://drive.redwood/reports/novadocs-poc-bench (shared spreadsheet), bit.ly/nd-poc-sample

[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — is this time still good?
[00:08] Marta: Yep, good here. We pushed a couple of overnight runs so I wanna make sure we go over TTFT numbers.
[00:12] Priya: Great, I pulled the latest runs and also a short streaming trace Samir uploaded. There's some interesting noise at small sequences.
[00:20] Samir: Sorry if the trace's messy — I anonymized things but you might see some odd spikes where clients retry.
[00:27] Jordan: Main ask from our side: we need median under 120ms for interactive editor flows and p99 under 600ms. Right now p99's creeping up to 1.2s on bursts.
[00:38] Alex: Noted. Is that across hosted or your private VM?
[00:41] Samir: This is hitting the Dedicated test pool you provisioned, the one with A100-equivalents. Under steady state it's fine, but bursts from our autoscaler create cold contexts.

[03:05] Priya: Ok, first slide — TTFT. On the run from last night, baseline (no streaming) median was 95ms, p95 220ms, p99 about 680ms. When we enabled streaming with a chunk size of 64 tokens the median was similar but p99 jumped.
[03:35] Marta: Is that because of the chunking implementation or because of kernel scheduling?
[03:39] Priya: Likely both. We're seeing scheduling latencies when small requests interleave with long sequences. Also the kernel choice interacts; the FP16 kernel we've been testing is faster for long runs but has slightly higher startup cost for the first token with our current compilation flags.
[04:12] Evan: To paraphrase, streaming helps average latency but hurts tail in mixed workloads. That's what we suspected.
[04:19] Samir: Yeah that matches our logs — lots of short completion requests (seq<100) during interactive editing.

[06:00] Marta: Curious — what's the effect if we reduce seq_len max or change the chunk size to 32?
[06:08] Priya: We ran a quick sweep: chunk=32 reduced p99 by ~150ms in that test, but throughput dropped slightly because we lost some batching efficiency. There's a tradeoff.
[06:28] Alex: Also on the server side, increasing the batching window from 10ms to 25ms captured more tokens into one batch which improved tokens/sec by ~12% but increased median by ~15ms.
[06:45] Jordan: Do you have plots for that?
[06:47] Priya: Yes — I uploaded delta plots to the sheet (see tab "batch-window-sweeps").

[09:10] Marta: The p99 at 1.2s was during a synthetic spike where we had ~40 concurrent short requests. Is there a cache warm-up effect?
[09:20] Priya: There is a KV cache warm-up pattern. For long sessions, the KV cache hits reduce token compute time. Short sessions rarely leverage the cache. We can look into prefix caching heuristics for short edits to warm-up frequently used prefixes.
[09:38] Samir: We can also route short tokens to a smaller-model fast path if Redwood supports model variants.
[09:44] Evan: Yes, smart routing is on the table — route <128 tokens to a trimmed variant with faster TTFT. We discussed earlier in the POC plan.

[12:05] Priya: Another note — the compiled kernel flavor we've been testing uses fused-attention kernels optimized for long seqs; it has a cold-start compile penalty in the runtime pipeline. We can use a warm compile strategy to pre-warm certain kernels at deployment time. That reduces first-token cost but increases startup overhead during deploy.
[12:30] Alex: We briefly tried preloading kernels in the staging pool; it shaved off ~60ms from initial token in our microbench.

[15:00] Marta: For our production risk posture, we prefer minimal changes that don't touch the model weights or prompt engineering. So kernel toggles and batching/window tweaks are ideal.
[15:12] Evan: Understood — we'll prioritize runtime-level changes.

[18:20] Priya: Proposed experiment list: 1) kernel/quant sweep (FP16 vs int8-like quant options) with seq len 128/512/1024; 2) streaming chunk sizes 32/64/128; 3) batching window 10/25/50ms; 4) warm kernel preload test. We'll run combos but focus on short-request tail.
[18:48] Samir: Good, please include a heatmap of p50/p95/p99 across combinations — that'll help us pick the sweet spot.

[21:05] Marta: Are there any known regressions with quantization causing hallucination-like differences for our use case? We do have guarded prompts but quality is important.
[21:15] Priya: In prior tests quantization to int8-like fast paths had minor score drift on open-ended tasks; for slot-filling/editor completions we saw minimal diffs. But we will add a small prompt-set regen test to ensure no quality regressions.

[24:00] Jordan: On the Dedicated vs Hosted cost question — can you give a quick range for the bursty config?
[24:07] Evan: Sure. For your current commit, Hosted on-demand nodes would cost roughly 2.4x per token at p50 throughput for bursts; Dedicated with burst capacity and reserved baseline gives ~1.3x per token relative to baseline hosted. I'll send precise numbers after this call.
[24:30] Samir: Important — what about autoscaling cooldowns? During spikes we saw new nodes come up but traffic still hit the old pool.
[24:40] Alex: We recommend a mix of pre-warmed warm-pools plus autoscale. The smaller warm pool prevents cold-start kernel compile and KV cache misses for the common editor prefixes.

[27:10] Priya: Quick note on metrics — we instrumented TTFT at the token emission hook; sometimes instrumentation skew happens if client merges streaming frames. So please check trace alignment in the sheet.
[27:30] Samir: Got it, will validate before we publish the logs.

[30:00] Marta: Any blockers on Redwood's side to run the kernel sweep?
[30:05] Priya: We have access to the kernels and quant paths in the test pool. The only blocker is if you want us to tune compilation flags or pre-warm specific kernels we need to know which model variants to prioritize.
[30:20] Jordan: Prioritize the editor model variant (editor-v2). Also include a smaller trimmed variant for short requests.

[33:00] Evan: So to recap action items — Priya will run the kernel/quant sweep with the sequence buckets and stream chunk sizes, Alex will spin up the second pool to test batch window, Samir will export anonymized traces, and I'll follow up on cost/SLA.
[33:18] Priya: One more technical caveat — when we reduce chunk size to 32 we increase network overhead for small frames; if your front-end aggregates too aggressively it might mask gains.
[33:35] Marta: We're using websockets and currently flush per chunk; we can modify client-side aggregator if needed.

[36:40] Jordan: Timeline — we'd like to lock a configuration by end of next week if possible. Can Redwood commit to that cadence?
[36:50] Evan: Yes, if we get logs and you sign off on the safety checks we'll aim to have recommended config by 2025-06-20.

[38:10] Samir: Also can you include a short note about SOC2 and audit logs for Dedicated? Our compliance team asked earlier.
[38:20] Evan: I'll attach the SOC2 excerpt and the audit log retention options to the follow-up email.

[40:00] Marta: Cool. Any final questions?
[40:05] Alex: No further questions. We'll start runs after Samir posts the traces.
[40:12] Jordan: Thanks all.
[40:18] Evan: Thanks everyone, we'll send the notes and schedule a mid-week sync if needed.

Meeting end ~16:42 UTC

Recap (auto):
- Key issues: p99 spikes on bursty short requests when streaming enabled.
- Hypotheses: kernel startup/compile + scheduling interference + KV cache warm-up.
- Experiments agreed: kernel/quant sweep, stream chunk sweep, batch window sweep, pre-warm kernels, add trimmed model route for short requests.
- Next meeting: tentatively 2025-06-17 pending results.

References shared in call: https://drive.redwood/reports/novadocs-poc-bench, bit.ly/nd-poc-sample
